sources.title: Colony Breeding: The Easiest Way to Breed Livebearers for Profit
Pregnant Guppy Fish: How To Tell & What To Do…

facts.fact: Guppies are livebearers: eggs are fertilized and hatch inside the female, and she gives birth to fully formed, functional fry.
Livebearers have fewer, larger fry than egg-layers because the fry must be able to survive on their own from birth.
Males fertilize females internally with the gonopodium, a modified anal fin. Mating is brief and can look like aggression.
Gestation usually lasts 21 to 31 days, occasionally up to 35. Water temperature, food and the mother's health affect the timing.
Litters range from 10 to 50 fry.
Litters range from 5 to 80 fry.
Litter size is 5–30 fry in one place in this article, and commonly 20–50 fry by strain elsewhere in the same article. Full Gold guppies are pregnant for about 25–35 days.
Females can store sperm for about ten months and can conceive again within hours of giving birth.
Females reach sexual maturity at around six weeks old.
The gravid spot behind the anal fin darkens and grows as the fry develop, and is nearly black just before birth. Tiny dots, the fry's eyes, may show through near term.
Over several weeks the belly swells and may become boxy or angular.
Dropsy and swim bladder disease can also swell the belly. The gravid spot is the key way to tell pregnancy apart from them.
Near birth a female may stop eating, hide, breathe laboriously or convulse.
By days 18–25 the belly looks square and distended. In the last days the fry's eyes are visible through the mother's skin.
In labor the female may rub against plants, shake and breathe heavily. When hiding places are scarce she may stay near the surface.
Healthy newborn fry swim upward, while stillborn fry sink to the bottom.
A female close to giving birth often looks sluggish, trembles and refuses food.
Birth takes about 2 to 6 hours.
Some births are over within three hours. Labor lasting more than twelve hours is rare and seldom produces healthy fry.
Poor water conditions can delay birth or end the pregnancy.
Moving a female who is close to giving birth may cause abortion or death.
Move the female to a separate breeding tank or breeder box once she is visibly pregnant. About 10 gallons is a practical tank size.
Many keepers separate the female around day 18–25 of pregnancy. Close to labor, a divider is suggested instead of moving her.
Give the fry cover: slanted-bottom breeder boxes, breeding mesh, or fine-leaved plants such as Java moss and hornwort.
Separate the fry from adults, because adults, including the parents, tend to eat them.
Use a small nursery tank with cover, conditions like the main tank, and gentle filtration that cannot suck in fry. A hanging nursery box with fine mesh is another option.
After birth, remove the mother and any stillborn fry.
Keep the mother apart for a day or two to recover before putting her back in the main tank.
Feed fry commercial baby fish food, finely crushed flakes, or tiny live or frozen foods.
Feed baby brine shrimp first. Infusoria or powdered fish food are alternatives.
Raise the fry separately for about two to three months before they join a community tank.
In colony breeding, fry stay in the adult tank and survive in thick plants. Use sponge filters, or a pre-filter sponge over the intake, so babies are not sucked up.
Feed fry small foods several times a day, such as baby brine shrimp, crushed flakes, daphnia and fry food. Adjust portions so leftover food does not rot.
Keep one male for every two to three females. This reduces stress on the females.
Remove fry with defects such as bent backs or missing fins. Repeat every few weeks, because some defects appear later.
Letting extra food rot and foul the water is a common mistake.
In very soft water, skipping minerals such as Wonder Shell or Seachem Equilibrium can lead to livebearer disease or 'shimmies'.
Adding salt can harm live plants. Moving fish raised in brackish water straight into fresh water can cause osmotic shock.
Vietnamese sources recommend feeding fry fine INVE powder food and bobo (water fleas) from 1–2 days old.
A Vietnamese guide suggests a frame of fine nylon or monofilament net with small mesh, so fry slip through while adults stay out.
The same guide suggests keeping water at 28–30°C to prevent disease, and treating water 2–3 days before adding fish.
A Vietnamese guide gives 24–28°C as a suitable temperature for guppies.
Change 20–30% of the water regularly so the fry grow quickly.
Endler's guppy (cá bảy màu rừng) has only 1–20 fry per litter.
Pregnant females often chase males and may nip their fins.
